Daniel usefully groups three phenomena under a shared intuition—local reactions that amplify upstream volatility—but the post blurs an important distinction: “bullwhip” is not just oscillation; it’s *information and decision latency* interacting with buffering policies. In the Beer Game, amplification typically comes from delayed signals, forecast updating, order batching, and safety-stock heuristics; the same demand can look increasingly noisy as it moves upstream even when every actor is “rational” under limited information (a classic system-dynamics point in [Sterman’s *Business Dynamics*](https://www.sterman.com/books/business-dynamics/) and earlier in Forrester). Traffic, by contrast, is less about misreading demand and more about *string instability* in a coupled dynamical system: small speed perturbations grow because drivers’ reaction times and acceleration constraints create unstable feedback. That’s why “phantom traffic jams” can arise on a circular track with constant density, as in the well-known experiment by [Sugiyama et al. (2008)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0968090X08000279). The family resemblance is real—delayed negative feedback can generate oscillations—but collapsing them into “PDE systems have attractors” is too coarse: point equilibria are themselves attractors; what Daniel seems to mean is a *limit cycle* emerging via a stability change (often described via Hopf bifurcation), and naming that mechanism would sharpen the claim.

The restaurant queue example is the most original, and it points toward queueing models with *balking* (not joining) and *reneging* (leaving after joining). But Daniel’s explanation relies on a hidden assumption: customers infer expected wait primarily from the *recent rate* of numbers being called, and do so similarly enough to synchronize their join/leave decisions. In practice, the “speed of number rolling” is also driven by table-size mismatches, batching by the host (“call 5 parties at once”), no-shows, and capacity shifts (a large table frees up, kitchen slows, etc.), which can create periodicity even without any perception feedback. If Daniel’s goal is a remedy, “reporting I’m leaving” is an information-structure intervention analogous to supply-chain demand-sharing: it could damp oscillations *if* the oscillation is expectation-driven rather than service-driven. A cleaner next step would be to separate (1) service process variability from (2) customer-belief feedback, and ask which dominates—because each implies a different fix.
